assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength optical lattice proposal removed Doppler and recoil shifts for many atoms at once, and the clocks now reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is the type of precision that opens new tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. As a laser spectroscopist I regard it as a clear case where better measurement creates new physics reach.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the original lattice-clock proposal and early demonstrations; Ye's group brought the clock to record accuracy and drove many of the comparisons and applications. The two-name list is compact and fair, though Hall and Hänsch (comb) already took the 2005 prize and other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr, Hinkley) contributed to the stability record. I would not add anyone from this credited list.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs in several countries have confirmed performance at the 1e-18 level and intercompared clocks. The interpretation is stable and the technique is already in use, so recognition is timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: The credited list leaves out strontium-clock contributors from other groups, so the 'decisive' set is a judgment call.
Ytterbium and other lattice species make the lead attribution somewhat diffuse.
I am relying on recalled uncertainty figures and have not verified them against the primary papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned cold-atom systems into tunable quantum simulators, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later quantum gas microscopy of Hubbard physics. The conceptual and experimental reach into many-body physics is very large, and the toolbox rests on control of light-atom interactions that I know well.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) supplied the theory proposal; Bloch and Greiner carried out the 2002 Mott-insulator experiment and Bloch led later lattice work; Esslinger realised fermionic Hubbard physics and the Mott insulator with fermions. Greiner is credited but, given the three-laureate limit, I leave him out; this is a real tension. Zoller also appears on the trapped-ion candidate, so the same person could not fairly count twice.
assessment.maturity: The platform is mature, reproduced worldwide and now yields quantitative results beyond classical simulation in some regimes. Recognition is timely, though BEC (2001) and optical-lattice precedents mean the committee needs a clear line to what is new.
uncertainties: Whether Greiner belongs ahead of Esslinger or Zoller is unresolved.
Overlap with the BEC prize and with trapped-ion and Rydberg simulators complicates scope.
Quantum advantage claims for analogue simulation are still being debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling to superconducting circuits and underpins most present superconducting quantum processors, with dispersive readout and strong-coupling physics central to the field. The impact on quantum information hardware is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory paper (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the Wallraff et al. strong-coupling experiment form the core. Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin give a sensible three-person configuration, leaving Blais out, which is a defensible but real omission. Attribution relative to the earlier Nakamura, Devoret and Martinis circuit work also needs care.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many laboratories and industrially deployed. The field has already received recognition for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, so the committee must justify a distinct scope, but the maturity of cQED itself is high.
uncertainties: Overlap with previously recognised superconducting-circuit work needs a careful scope statement.
Blais's exclusion may be contested.
The charge-qubit versus cavity-based lineage is a matter of interpretation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for a trapped-ion quantum gate and the experimental realisations with entangled ions established a leading platform for quantum computing and simulation. It builds directly on ion trapping and laser cooling, areas close to my own spectroscopy background.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the theory originators and Blatt is a leading experimentalist for scalable ion processors, but Wineland's group demonstrated the first gate and shared the 2012 prize, so the credit boundary is delicate. Zoller recurs on the optical-lattice simulation candidate and Cirac on the cavity-QED network candidate, so the set of overlapping candidates would need a single coordinated treatment.
assessment.maturity: Experimental platforms are mature with high-fidelity gates and repeated cross-laboratory confirmation. Recognition is plausible now, though the 2012 prize narrows the novelty argument.
uncertainties: The 2012 prize to Wineland reduces the marginal discovery under consideration.
Partial overlap in personnel with the cavity-QED network and optical-lattice simulation candidates.
Whether Blatt or other experimentalists such as Monroe or Wineland-linked groups are the right third name is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics reached ground-state cooling and quantum control of macroscopic mechanical oscillators, enabling quantum-limited sensing and mechanical quantum memories and transducers. This is important for measurement physics and fits the theme that quantum sensors extend what can be measured.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Cleland each hold decisive and distinct milestones (radiation-pressure cooling, strong coupling and ground-state work, quantum-state control of a mechanical resonator), though other groups including Painter, Lehnert and Harris contributed and are not on the credited list. The three-person split is workable but incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Results are reproduced across platforms, but the field is still developing toward applications, so recognition is moderately early.
uncertainties: Omitted contributors such as Painter, Lehnert and Harris weaken the attribution.
Applications remain largely prospective.
Impact on fundamental physics is still evolving.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry underlies precision measurements of gravity, rotation and the fine-structure constant and tests of the equivalence principle, and it grew out of laser cooling and coherent atom optics. The reach into metrology is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich are plausible originators of key demonstration lines (atom beam interferometers, Ramsey-Bordé interferometry, light-pulse gravimeters). The history is distributed across several groups, including Chu, Mlynek and Rasel, and the credited names omit some. This is a difficult attribution.
assessment.maturity: Techniques are mature and widely used, but the discovery is more of a methodology than a single result, and the physics reach (e.g. large-scale tests) is still being built.
uncertainties: Distributed credit across many groups.
The 1997 and 2001 prizes already cover cooling and condensates, narrowing the novelty argument.
Whether the contribution is a discovery or a technique is unsettled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Laser excitation of the thorium-229 isomer opens a nuclear clock with potential sensitivity to variations of fundamental constants and new physics. It is conceptually striking and is the type of measurement advance I value, with clear scientific upside.
assessment.attribution: Peik proposed the nuclear clock idea; Schumm's group, and the Ye collaboration with the Vienna group, achieved the 2024 laser excitation. Other contributors (Thirolf, Tiedau, Beeks, Zhang) are not on the list. Ye also appears on the optical-lattice clock candidate, which complicates parallel recognition.
assessment.maturity: The key result is recent and the clock itself has not yet been shown to match optical-lattice performance. Recognition would be premature relative to confirmed stability.
uncertainties: Premature without demonstrated clock operation.
Credit for the 2024 excitation is shared across several teams not all on the list.
Ye overlap with the optical-lattice clock candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The ATLAS and CMS observation of the Higgs boson completed the Standard Model and is plainly of fundamental importance. The experimental discovery rests on detector concepts that took decades to build.
assessment.attribution: Prize recognition for large collaborations is difficult. Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are leaders of the proposals and construction of ATLAS and CMS, but the discovery itself was a collective effort of thousands, and the 2013 prize already honoured the theoretical prediction. I see the credit as defensible but contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by two experiments and measured further at the LHC. The interpretation is stable; timing is acceptable though a decade after the first prize.
uncertainties: Fairness of crediting spokespersons or founders for a collective discovery.
Whether the 2013 prize already settled the main recognition.
I am not asserting the internal history of the collaborations.
